ENT / Otolaryngology Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger: Acute breathing difficulty and lip tingling ~15 min after a wasp sting sustained while gardening.
- Symptom timeline/progression: Sudden onset within minutes; symptoms ongoing at time of call.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat: denies sensation of throat closing, no dysphagia/odynophagia, no voice change.  
  • Mouth/lips: tingling; patient “can feel something” in lips; no definite swelling reported.  
  • Nose/eyes: not mentioned.  
  • Airway: shallow breathing, chest tightness; no stridor/noisy breathing reported.  
  • Drooling: not reported.  
  • Ear/neck: no complaints.
- Cutaneous: blotchy skin rash noted by patient.
- Relevant past episodes/treatment: No prior similar reactions; no previous ED visits or epinephrine use for stings.
- Allergies: Penicillin. Wasp venom sensitivity not previously known. 
- Current medications: Antihistamines PRN for flying-related aerosinusitis (dose/route/frequency not documented). No regular long-term medications.
- Past medical history: Eczema; history of aerosinusitis with flights. No asthma or other chronic respiratory disease reported.
- Social context: Wife present; able to call ambulance as instructed.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: Tingling of lips only; no definite lip/throat/facial swelling described.
- Airway/breathing: Patient reports shallow breathing and chest tightness; no stridor or audible wheeze noted in remote interaction.
- Mental status: Alert and conversational.
- Vitals/examination: Not recorded (remote consultation).
- Companion: Wife present and facilitating ambulance call.

Assessment:
- Working impression: Suspected early anaphylactic reaction to wasp sting with respiratory involvement (shallow breathing, chest tightness) and cutaneous features (blotchy rash, lip tingling).
  Evidence: Immediate onset after sting; multisystem symptoms; physician concern and emergency referral.
- DDx integration (consistent with transcript):
  1. Anaphylaxis secondary to wasp sting – high likelihood: rapid multisystem reaction; potential to progress; warrants EMS.
     • Opposing evidence: No documented lip/throat swelling, hypotension, or GI symptoms yet.
  2. Systemic allergic urticaria without full anaphylaxis – moderate likelihood: cutaneous rash and tingling present; respiratory symptoms could still evolve (**monitor closely**).
  3. Anxiety-related hyperventilation – low likelihood: could explain shallow breathing; contradicted by objective rash.  
  (No conflict between transcript and DDx.)

Plan:
- Immediate actions:
  • Advised patient’s wife to call emergency medical services (ambulance) rather than self-transport.  
  • Instructed administration of available oral antihistamine while awaiting EMS.
- Patient/caregiver instructions:
  • Remain seated, stay with wife, avoid exertion.  
  • If worsening breathing, throat tightness, dizziness, or swelling occurs before EMS arrival, lie flat with legs elevated if tolerated and inform dispatch immediately.
- Escalation criteria/red flags: Increased breathing difficulty, voice change, throat closing sensation, lip/tongue/facial swelling, syncope, or spreading rash.
- Follow-up:
  • Emergency department evaluation now.  
  • After acute care, advised to seek allergy/ENT referral for venom immunotherapy discussion and prescription of epinephrine auto-injector if confirmed insect-sting anaphylaxis.  
  • Avoid gardening/bee-wasp exposure until formally assessed.
- COVID-19 vaccine: Not discussed.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing expected elements: objective vitals (HR, BP, RR, SpO₂), direct visualization of airway, confirmation of sting site, details of antihistamine (name/dose), past reactions to stings, availability of epinephrine auto-injector, comprehensive allergy list.  
● Transcript/DDx conflicts: none noted.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; minor conversational overlaps; no significant inaudible sections.
